1.d4 e6 2.c4.strategy: Adds the c-pawn to the fight for d5 and keeps the whole range of Queen's Gambit and Indian set-ups available. White claims space in the centre while Black, who has shown little so far, still chooses what kind of game it becomes: classical and solid, or counter-attacking. The cost is that the c-pawn is committed and the d4-pawn is guarded only by pieces.

1.d4 e6 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops the king's knight, guards d4 and e5 and commits to nothing else, so every set-up stays open: a flexible, solid start that reaches much the same range of games as 2.c4. The price is that White leaves it to Black to decide how sharp the game gets.

1.d4 e6 2.e4.strategy: Builds the full pawn centre and invites the French Defence, often a game of locked pawn chains and slow manoeuvring. White gets space and an early grip on the centre, but the d4-pawn gives Black a clear target to attack.

1.d4 e6 2.Bf4.strategy: Develops the dark-squared bishop before e3 can shut it in, the first step of the London System: a solid, easily learned set-up with a fixed plan that works against almost any reply. The cost is that b2 loses its guard, so Black can target it.

1.d4 e6 2.g3.strategy: Prepares Bg2 on the long diagonal, aimed at d5 and b7, for a slow set-up with the king's bishop fianchettoed. It is slower than the natural central moves, so Black can strike at d4 or settle the centre first.

1.d4 e6 2.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight and keeps the e4 advance available, with a broad pawn centre in view. The knight blocks the c-pawn, so White cannot build the centre with it, and ...Bb4 pins the knight at once. Sound, but less flexible than the natural alternatives.

1.d4 e6 2.Nd2.strategy: Supports e4 to build a broad pawn centre. The knight shuts in the c1-bishop, which takes Bf4 away, and Black is free to choose any set-up. Playable but passive.

1.d4 e6 2.c3.strategy: Props up d4 and stops ...Bb4+ for a compact set-up. It is slow and takes c3 from the b1-knight, which must come out via d2, while Black develops freely. Sound, but it gives up the initiative.

1.d4 e6 2.e3.strategy: Frees the f1-bishop and supports d4 for a compact set-up. It shuts the c1-bishop in behind the pawn, however, and Black takes the centre at no cost. Sound but committal, since developing the knight first keeps the option of Bf4 before e3.

1.d4 e6 2.b3.strategy: Prepares Bb2, but with the pawn already on d4 the bishop only supports its own pawn until the diagonal opens later. Black can simply develop and take the centre. Playable, but the natural central moves do more for the centre.

1.d4 e6 2.a3.strategy: Stops ...Bb4+ and prepares b4, but it develops nothing and loses a tempo. Black takes the centre at once while White's pieces are still at home.

1.d4 e6 2.a4.strategy: A rim pawn move that neither develops a piece nor fights for the centre, and it does not even stop ...Bb4+. Black simply takes the centre and has a free game.

1.d4 e6 2.b4.strategy: Prepares Bb2, but the pawn is undefended and 2...Bxb4+ takes it with check. White has only a little development for the lost pawn.

1.d4 e6 2.f3.strategy: Prepares e4 but takes f3 from the g1-knight and opens the e1-h4 diagonal, so 2...Qh4+ forces the weakening 3.g3 or a king move that loses castling. The move does nothing against Black taking the centre.

1.d4 e6 2.f4.strategy: Takes control of e5 but develops no piece and opens the e1-h4 diagonal, so 2...Qh4+ forces the weakening 3.g3 or a king move. Black is then free to build the centre.

1.d4 e6 2.g4.strategy: Gains space on the kingside but leaves the pawn undefended: 2...Qh4 attacks it at once, pins the f2-pawn and forces White to defend it. The kingside is loosened before a single piece has developed.

1.d4 e6 2.h3.strategy: A waiting move that does nothing for the centre or development. Black is free to build the centre unhindered.

1.d4 e6 2.h4.strategy: A flank thrust that does nothing for the centre or development and loosens the kingside without a target. White has lost a tempo, and Black replies ...d5 with an easy game.

1.d4 e6 2.Bd2.strategy: Takes d2 from the b1-knight and puts the bishop on a passive square, where it does less than it would on f4. Black develops freely and takes the centre.

1.d4 e6 2.Be3.strategy: Blocks the e-pawn completely, since e2-e4 needs e3 to be empty, so while the bishop stands there the f1-bishop can only come out via g3 and Bg2. The move does not challenge the centre, and Black takes space there.

1.d4 e6 2.Qd2.strategy: An early queen move that blocks the c1-bishop, takes d2 from the b1-knight and develops nothing. 2...Bb4 attacks the queen at once, so White must move it again or block, and Black takes the centre.

1.d4 e6 2.Qd3.strategy: Brings the queen out early and blocks the f1-bishop's diagonal. Black can gain time by attacking the queen and pressing d4, while White has no development to show for the queen's trip.

1.d4 e6 2.Nh3.strategy: A rim knight heading for f4, where it would press on e6, but it stands far from the centre and leaves the natural f3-square unused. Black simply takes the centre with ...d5.

1.d4 e6 2.Na3.strategy: Heads for c4 or b5 from the rim and does nothing against the centre. Black can take the centre at once, or take with 2...Bxa3 3.bxa3, doubling and isolating White's a-pawns at the cost of the bishop pair.

1.d4 e6 2.d5.strategy: Exchanges the d-pawn for the e-pawn at once: after 2...exd5 3.Qxd5 the queen stands exposed in the centre, and Black develops with gain of time.

1.d4 e6 2.Kd2.strategy: Forfeits castling and puts the king in the open centre, where 2...Bb4+ gains time and the king blocks the c1-bishop and the queen. White gains nothing for the lasting weakness.

1.d4 e6 2.Bg5.strategy: Hangs the bishop: the queen's diagonal d8-g5 is open after ...e6, nothing defends the bishop, and 2...Qxg5 wins a piece.

1.d4 e6 2.Bh6.strategy: Loses the bishop for nothing: 2...gxh6 or 2...Nxh6 takes it and nothing recaptures.

1.d4 e6.name: Franco-Indian Defence
1.d4 e6.background: The name reflects that 1...e6 may lead to the French Defence or to one of the Indian Defences. Eric Schiller proposed calling it the Horwitz Defence, after Bernhard Horwitz, who played it against Daniel Harrwitz between 1849 and 1852.

1.d4 e6 2.Bf4 Nf6.strategy: Develops a piece, controls e4 and d5 and commits Black to nothing else: the pawn structure can still become a solid central one, a fianchetto set-up or an early pawn break against d4. The c8-bishop stays shut in behind e6 until the b-pawn frees it.

1.d4 e6 2.Bf4 d5.strategy: Takes a share of the centre and heads for a solid, classical game. Black has a solid structure and plenty of room to develop, and the bishop on f4 is not a threat to it. The cost is the c8-bishop, which the e6-pawn shuts in and which often struggles to find a good square.

1.d4 e6 2.Bf4 c5.background: Black's most common response to the London System involves ...c5 and ...Qb6, and an early ...c5 is described as popular at higher levels of play. With ...Nf6 instead of ...e6, Johnsen and Kovačević considered 1.d4 Nf6 2.Bf4 c5 3.e3 Qb6 the most critical line.
1.d4 e6 2.Bf4 c5.strategy: Strikes at d4 at once and exploits the bishop's absence from c1: the b2-pawn is undefended, so a queen on b6 hits it. This is a popular way to disturb White's comfortable set-up. Black gets quick queenside play and active development, while the c8-bishop is still shut in behind e6.

1.d4 e6 2.Bf4 f5.background: The English grandmaster Simon Williams often uses 1.d4 e6 as a way of playing for the Dutch Defence while avoiding the Staunton Gambit, 1.d4 f5 2.e4.
1.d4 e6 2.Bf4 f5.strategy: Controls e4 and heads for a Dutch set-up, flexible between the king's bishop on e7 and a Stonewall pawn wall. Black plays for the initiative on the kingside. The advance weakens e6 and the e8-h5 diagonal, and the e5-square, which the f4-bishop already covers, can become an outpost for a white knight.

1.d4 e6 2.Bf4 Bd6.strategy: Offers the bishop trade, but 3.Bxd6 can only be answered by ...cxd6, since the d7-pawn blocks the queen's recapture. That doubles Black's d-pawns and leaves the c8-bishop shut in behind them, and White gets the better structure.

1.d4 e6 2.Bf4 Be7.strategy: Prepares castling, but the bishop is passive on e7 and does not challenge the f4-bishop as it would from d6. White builds freely or claims the centre with 3.e4.

1.d4 e6 2.Bf4 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece and attacks d4, but blocks the c-pawn, so the usual ...c5 break against the London is no longer available. White keeps a solid centre and a comfortable set-up. Sound, but it offers less than a developing move that keeps the c-pawn free.

1.d4 e6 2.Bf4 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7 on the long diagonal. It is flexible but gives White a free hand in the centre: White can build a broad pawn centre that Black must undermine later.

1.d4 e6 2.Bf4 g6.strategy: Prepares ...Bg7 for a fianchetto set-up, keeping central pawn breaks in reserve. It is sound, but White can build a broad centre with easy development, and the pawns on e6 and g6 leave f6 and h6 without pawn cover.

1.d4 e6 2.Bf4 Ne7.strategy: Prepares ...Ng6 to chase the f4-bishop and fits a compact set-up with a fianchetto. The knight shuts in the f8-bishop until it moves on, and the plan is slow: White can take the centre and simply retreat the bishop when it is chased.

1.d4 e6 2.Bf4 c6.strategy: Supports a later ...d5 behind a solid pawn chain and opens the d8-a5 diagonal for the queen. It is sound but slow: it develops no piece, and White can claim the centre or build a calm set-up.

1.d4 e6 2.Bf4 d6.strategy: Plays for a compact set-up with the pawns on d6 and e6 as a wall and the knights placed behind them. The pawn blocks the f8-bishop's diagonal, though, and White can take a broad centre against a cramped position.

1.d4 e6 2.Bf4 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it covers b4 and c5 but no central square. White takes the centre, which also opens the f1-bishop's diagonal, so Bxa6 bxa6 can double Black's a-pawns.

1.d4 e6 2.Bf4 Nh6.strategy: Heads for f5 from the rim, but the bishop on f4 attacks it: 3.Bxh6 gxh6 wrecks Black's kingside pawns for the bishop pair. Even without the exchange the knight is far from the centre.

1.d4 e6 2.Bf4 a6.strategy: A waiting move on the wing that is sound but slow: it develops no piece and does nothing for the centre, and at most prepares ...b5. White develops freely or takes the centre.

1.d4 e6 2.Bf4 a5.strategy: Gains space on the wing but weakens b5, where a white knight would eye c7 and d6, and does nothing for the centre or development. White continues to develop at leisure.

1.d4 e6 2.Bf4 b5.strategy: Gains queenside space, which is sound, but the pawn is loose: 3.Nc3, or 3.e4 opening the f1-bishop's path, attacks it at once, so Black must spend a tempo on it. The advance also weakens c6.

1.d4 e6 2.Bf4 h6.strategy: Takes g5 from White's pieces and prepares ...g5 to chase the f4-bishop, but develops nothing and loosens the kingside. Sound, yet White builds a full set-up while Black does nothing for the centre.

1.d4 e6 2.Bf4 h5.strategy: Advances the rook's pawn without developing a piece or contesting d4, and rules out ...h6 against a bishop on g5. White develops freely or takes the centre.

1.d4 e6 2.Bf4 f6.strategy: Takes f6 from the g8-knight, develops nothing and opens the e8-h5 diagonal to the black king, so Qh5+ becomes possible once White's e-pawn has moved. White takes the centre, and the g8-knight is left with awkward squares.

1.d4 e6 2.Bf4 g5.strategy: Attacks the bishop with a pawn the queen guards, so 3.Bxg5 Qxg5 would lose a piece for a pawn. White simply retreats the bishop, and the advance has only loosened Black's kingside: f6 and h6 have lost their pawn cover, and g5 soon comes under attack again.

1.d4 e6 2.Bf4 Bb4+.strategy: The check gains nothing: 3.c3 blocks it with a move White wants anyway and attacks the bishop, which must retreat at the cost of a tempo.

1.d4 e6 2.Bf4 Qe7.strategy: Leaves c7 undefended, because the d7-pawn blocks the queen's guard along the seventh rank, and shuts in the f8-bishop. After 3.Bxc7 Black regains the pawn with 3...Qb4+ and ...Qxb2, but the queen wanders further while White develops.

1.d4 e6 2.Bf4 Ke7.strategy: Gives up castling at once and shuts in the f8-bishop. 3.Bg5+ then forces a block or another king move, and the king never finds a safe home on e7.

1.d4 e6 2.Bf4 e5.strategy: Pushes the pawn into capture: e5 is attacked by the d4-pawn and the bishop and defended by nothing, so 3.dxe5 or 3.Bxe5 simply wins a pawn.

1.d4 e6 2.Bf4 Bc5.strategy: Hangs the bishop to 3.dxc5, and nothing recaptures on c5, since no black pawn or piece covers it. White wins a whole piece for nothing.

1.d4 e6 2.Bf4 Ba3.strategy: Walks into a capture: 3.bxa3 or 3.Nxa3 wins the bishop for nothing, since a3 is covered by the b2-pawn and the knight on b1 and Black has no follow-up.

1.d4 e6 2.Bf4 Qf6.strategy: Attacks the bishop on f4, but with the queen gone from d8 the c7-pawn is loose: 3.Bxc7 saves the bishop and wins a pawn. The queen also takes f6 from the g8-knight, so Black has little to show for the pawn.

1.d4 e6 2.Bf4 Qg5.strategy: Hangs the queen: the bishop on f4 attacks g5 and nothing defends it, so 3.Bxg5 wins the queen for nothing.

1.d4 e6 2.Bf4 Qh4.strategy: Attacks the bishop on f4, but with the queen gone from d8 the c7-pawn is undefended: 3.Bxc7 saves the bishop and wins a pawn, and White could instead gain time against the queen.

1.d4 e6 2.Bf4 f5 3.g4.name: Dutch Defence: Senechaud Gambit
1.d4 e6 2.Bf4 f5 3.g4.strategy: A gambit: the g-pawn is offered to open the kingside before any piece is developed. Black takes it and is a pawn up, but White's h3 hits the pawn at once and the open lines give enough play to keep the balance. Sound, yet it risks more than calm development.

1.d4 e6 2.Bf4 f5 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight to the square that matters most against ...f5, from where it watches e5, and keeps the centre and castling flexible. The bishop already stands outside the pawn chain, so White can complete a solid, harmonious set-up before choosing a plan.

1.d4 e6 2.Bf4 f5 3.e3.strategy: Solid and modest: the pawn guards d4 and the bishop on f4 and opens the way for the king's bishop. White builds a sturdy position without hurry, but gives up the quick e4 break and leaves Black the choice of set-up.

1.d4 e6 2.Bf4 f5 3.e4.strategy: Offers the e-pawn to open lines against Black's kingside, where ...f5 has left the diagonal to the king open, so a queen check is available at once. White gets activity for the pawn, but with best play no more than equality.

1.d4 e6 2.Nf3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight and controls e4 and d5, so Black can still choose between a classical set-up with a pawn on d5 and a flexible one with a fianchettoed or pinning bishop. The cost is the c8-bishop, shut in behind the e6-pawn until a pawn move frees it. A flexible, solid reply that lets White decide how sharp the game gets.

1.d4 e6 2.Nf3 d5.strategy: Takes a share of the centre at once and builds a solid pawn chain, with the knight and bishop to develop behind it. Black accepts a slightly cramped position: the c8-bishop is shut in behind the e6-pawn until the centre opens or ...b6 is played. A sound, classical set-up for a quiet game.

1.d4 e6 2.Nf3 c5.strategy: Challenges d4 before White has built a big centre, and aims at an active game with play on the half-open c-file or d-file. If the centre opens, the d-pawn can end up backward and weak, and Black must develop fast to avoid being left behind. A more combative choice than the quiet set-ups.

1.d4 e6 2.Nf3 f5.name: Dutch Defence
1.d4 e6 2.Nf3 f5.background: Black sometimes begins with 1...e6 to reach the Dutch without allowing the Staunton Gambit (1.d4 f5 2.e4), named after Howard Staunton, who introduced it in his match against Bernhard Horwitz in London in 1846. English grandmaster Simon Williams often uses 1.d4 e6 for exactly this purpose.
1.d4 e6 2.Nf3 f5.strategy: Claims e4 and aims at an aggressive, unbalancing game on the kingside. The price is a weakened e8-h5 diagonal, and a white knight can settle on e5. Black plays for a win, and accepts real risk.

1.d4 e6 2.Nf3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a knight and adds pressure on d4, but blocks the c-pawn, so the ...c5 break has to wait. White simply builds the centre. Playable, but 2...Nf6 develops just as quickly without blocking the c-pawn.

1.d4 e6 2.Nf3 Be7.strategy: Develops the bishop and prepares quick castling, but commits the bishop before White's plan is known and gives up the ...Bb4+ option that 2...Nf6 keeps. White can take the centre and gain extra space. Sound, but less flexible than the main replies.

1.d4 e6 2.Nf3 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7 against e4 and the long diagonal. White can simply take the centre, and theory regards Black's set-up against it as dubious. Playable, not recommended.

1.d4 e6 2.Nf3 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 and a solid pawn chain. The c-pawn is committed before White's plan is clear, so White can sidestep it, and a later ...c5 would cost a second tempo. Sound, but less flexible than 2...Nf6 or 2...d5.

1.d4 e6 2.Nf3 d6.strategy: Opens d7 for the c8-bishop and the b8-knight and prepares a compact set-up with quick development and castling. White takes space, and Black has no quick way to challenge the centre. Sound but passive.

1.d4 e6 2.Nf3 g6.strategy: Prepares ...Bg7 and kingside castling, a fianchetto set-up behind the e6-pawn. No pawn contests d4 or e4 yet, so White has a free hand, and Black must later undermine the large centre with ...c5 or ...d5. Sound enough, but slower than 2...Nf6 or 2...d5.

1.d4 e6 2.Nf3 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it eyes b4 and c5 but does little else, and 3.e4 followed by Bxa6 would double Black's a-pawns. The centre is left to White, who simply takes space.

1.d4 e6 2.Nf3 Qe7.strategy: Blocks the f8-bishop and invites 3.Bg5, which develops with an attack on the queen: ...f6 weakens the kingside, and ...Nf6 walks into a pin. Black's other pieces stay at home while White develops with threats.

1.d4 e6 2.Nf3 Qf6.strategy: Brings the queen out early and takes f6 from the knight, and 3.Bg5 attacks it at once: 3...Qxg5 loses the queen to 4.Nxg5. White gains a tempo and a free hand in the centre.

1.d4 e6 2.Nf3 Bd6.strategy: Puts the bishop in front of the d-pawn, where 3.e4 and e5 will chase it. Developing the knight is no cure: 3.e4 Nf6 4.e5 forks the bishop on d6 and the knight on f6.

1.d4 e6 2.Nf3 Bb4+.strategy: Checks without a target: 3.c3 drives the bishop back at once, and 3.Bd2 or 3.Nbd2 blocks it with a developing move. Without a pawn on c4 the check gains nothing, and a trade on d2 only brings another white piece into play.

1.d4 e6 2.Nf3 Nh6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, from where 3.Bxh6 gxh6 wrecks the kingside pawns for a mere bishop-for-knight trade. Nothing is developed usefully and the h-pawns are doubled and isolated.

1.d4 e6 2.Nf3 Ne7.strategy: Prepares ...d5 and a regrouping of the knight but blocks the f8-bishop and the queen, and the knight stands worse on e7 than on f6. White takes the centre while Black's pieces stay tangled.

1.d4 e6 2.Nf3 a6.strategy: Takes b5 from White's pieces and prepares ...b5 and a bishop on b7. Nothing punishes it, but it spends a tempo on a rim pawn while the centre and development are untouched, so White develops freely.

1.d4 e6 2.Nf3 a5.strategy: Stops b4 and gains queenside space, but spends a tempo on a rim pawn and leaves b5 weak. Neither the centre nor development is addressed, so White simply gets on with development.

1.d4 e6 2.Nf3 b5.strategy: Grabs queenside space before any piece is out, and the pawn is loose: 3.e4 opens the f1-bishop and threatens Bxb5, and a4 can hit it as well. The c6-square is weakened, and White gains the centre at no cost.

1.d4 e6 2.Nf3 f6.strategy: Takes f6 from the knight, weakens the e8-h5 diagonal and develops nothing. White builds the centre at leisure, while the g8-knight is left with e7 or h6.

1.d4 e6 2.Nf3 h6.strategy: Stops Bg5, which would attack the queen, so the g8-knight can come out without a pin. It spends a tempo on a rim pawn and does nothing for the centre, so White simply takes space. Sound, but second-rate.

1.d4 e6 2.Nf3 h5.strategy: Develops nothing and weakens g6, and with the pawn already past h6 a bishop on g5 can no longer be driven away by ...h6. White uses the tempo to develop, and 3.Bg5 also hits the queen on d8.

1.d4 e6 2.Nf3 Qg5.strategy: Hangs the queen: both 3.Bxg5 and 3.Nxg5 capture it, and nothing defends g5 or recaptures.

1.d4 e6 2.Nf3 Qh4.strategy: Hangs the queen to 3.Nxh4, since nothing defends h4.

1.d4 e6 2.Nf3 Ke7.strategy: Gives up castling for nothing and walks into 3.Bg5+, which gains a tempo. The king in the open centre blocks the f8-bishop and the queen with no compensation.

1.d4 e6 2.Nf3 Bc5.strategy: Loses a piece to 3.dxc5, since the d-pawn attacks the bishop and nothing recaptures on c5.

1.d4 e6 2.Nf3 Ba3.strategy: Loses the bishop: 3.bxa3 or 3.Nxa3 captures it and Black gets nothing in return.

1.d4 e6 2.Nf3 g5.strategy: Hangs the pawn: 3.Bxg5 or 3.Nxg5 wins it, and recapturing with ...Qxg5 loses the queen to the other piece. The kingside is loosened for nothing.

1.d4 e6 2.Nf3 e5.strategy: Hangs the pawn: 3.dxe5 wins it, the knight on f3 guards the new pawn on e5, and Black has no quick way to regain it. White is simply a pawn up.
